metadata.title: Small-class effects on science achievement in secondary education

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-old students in 26 selected countries/economies, with analytic samples restricted to countries where the teacher-reported class size variable and the full set of propensity-score covariates were available. To address PISA’s complex sampling design (unequal probabilities of selection and nonresponse), the authors apply sampling weights in the propensity score (PS) analysis and in the subsequent outcome model. Specifically, they use the total student weight W_FSTUWT, and the PS-weighted treatment effect model uses a product of PS weights (ATT framework) and sampling weights. The paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and instead relies on robust standard errors to account for clustering in PISA.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is PISA 2015 science achievement measured using 10 plausible values (PV1SCIE–PV10SCIE). The paper describes combining the 10 PV-specific regression results using Schafer’s formula (a standard PV combining approach), but it does not explicitly document how missing data in covariates or outcomes were handled prior to estimation. Because the manuscript does not report whether missing covariate values were imputed or cases were excluded, the missing-data handling strategy cannot be verified from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study starts from PISA 2015 data covering 71 participating countries/economies, then excludes 45 countries and retains 26 countries/economies based on three criteria: (1) the teacher-reported class size variable is available; (2) the proportion of small classes (defined as 20 or fewer students) is at least 10% to ensure adequate overlap between small-class and non-small-class groups for propensity score analysis; and (3) the PS model covariates are available so that the same statistical model can be estimated across countries. The outcome is science achievement using PISA’s science literacy framework for 15-year-olds, and the analysis is run separately for each of the 10 science plausible values (PV1SCIE–PV10SCIE) and then combined.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Percent grade repeat students at school

main_findings.performance_metrics: Propensity score ATT with sampling weights: small classes show significant negative effects in 9/26 countries (e.g., Germany −0.32, Finland −0.06). Fixed-effects meta-analysis across 26 country estimates: δ = −0.05, SE = 0.01, p < 0.01, 95% CI [−0.07, −0.04]. Fixed-effects meta-analysis across 9 significant estimates: δ = −0.13, SE = 0.01, p < 0.01, 95% CI [−0.15, −0.11].
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 science data for 15-year-old students across 26 countries/economies, the study leveraged small class status (≤20 students) together with ESCS, test anxiety, inquiry-based practices, and school ESCS to estimate the ATT effect on PV-based science achievement, finding that small classes had a statistically significant but small negative average effect on science achievement (δ = −0.05, 95% CI [−0.07, −0.04]). This indicates that implementing class-size reduction policies in secondary science may not reliably improve science achievement and could even be counterproductive in some contexts, though effect sizes are small and causal assumptions depend on measured covariates and overlap.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 science achievement for 15-year-old students in 26 countries/economies (24 European plus the U.S. and Canada), using teacher-reported class size and defining “small classes” as 20 or fewer students. Science achievement is measured with 10 PISA plausible values (PV1SCIE–PV10SCIE), and the authors estimate propensity score (ATT) models with inverse probability of treatment weighting combined with PISA sampling weights (W_FSTUWT), then combine PV-specific estimates using Schafer’s formula. Across all 26 country estimates, the fixed-effects meta-analytic effect of small classes is δ = −0.05 (SE = 0.01, p < 0.01; 95% CI [−0.07, −0.04]); among the 9 countries with significant effects, δ = −0.13 (95% CI [−0.15, −0.11]). The paper reports robust standard errors for clustering and checks covariate balance before/after PS weighting, but it does not explicitly document missing-data handling for covariates/outcomes. Overall, the results suggest small-class policies do not consistently raise secondary science achievement and may vary substantially by country context.
